Evidence class: Contradicted — the repo's own timeout path falsifies the claimed capability (faulthandler frames carry no loop index, and warnings are not flushed by a worker that exits mid-call)
findings.finding: The plan says that if the test still times out, 'the banner's stack names the chunk', and that the spans tell a stall apart from per-object cost. On the timeout path the instrument provides neither. (1) `_ci_timed_call` reports through `warnings.warn(PytestWarning)` (conftest.py:48). pytest's warning capture records call-phase warnings only when the call phase ends. The crash guard's timer calls `pytest_timeout.timeout_timer`, which exits the xdist worker (`_crash_guard.py:69-86`, banner text 'the worker exits now'). So the spans of the `hash_object[k]` chunks that finished before the kill are never sent to the controller. (2) The banner's stack is a `faulthandler.dump_traceback` (`_crash_guard.py:85`), which prints file:line frames and no locals. Every `hash_object[k]` call in a loop shares one source line, so the dump cannot say which k stalled. In the timeout case, which is the outcome the plan most needs to tell apart, the measurement produces no chunk data.
findings.location: Approach step 1 (Measure) and AC 1 ('or a timeout stack naming a chunk')
scenarios: The Windows sweep after step 1 hits 600 s again (2 of the last 3 runs did). The log shows the banner and a stack at the single `hash_object` call line, but no `[rebar-ci-timing]` lines and no chunk index, so AC 1's 'progressing vs blocked' verdict cannot be recorded.
findings.suggested_fix: In step 1, give each of the 10 `git hash-object -w --stdin-paths` chunk calls a `timeout=` (e.g. 50 s) and catch `subprocess.TimeoutExpired` to `pytest.fail(f'hash_object[{k}] did not finish in 50 s after chunks 0..{k-1}')`. The test then fails inside its call phase before the 600 s pytest-timeout. pytest flushes the earlier `[rebar-ci-timing]` spans, and the failure message names the stalled chunk. Update the Approach and AC 1 wording to read the chunk from that failure message, not from the timeout banner.

findings.finding: Step 1 has no decision consequence, and its chunking measures a different configuration from the one that failed. Step 2 is unconditional: the fill is removed whatever step 1 finds. The plan's only reason for measuring first ('so that the cause is measured on Windows before the fill is removed') never says which result would change the plan. The plan's own evidence already rules out a Python-side pipe deadlock ('all 3 pipes have a live Python thread servicing them'), which means git itself was not reading stdin. Splitting one 20,000-path git process into ten 2,000-path processes also changes the conditions of the failing run: one long-lived process with a ~2 MB stdin. A cost tied to that single long run would not reproduce, and the chunked run would read as 'progressing'. So the measurement may misattribute the cause, and it adds a CI round-trip plus a non-codebase gate that the fix does not depend on.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Extend the dispatch guard to also wait on queued runs (e.g. `gh run list --workflow test.yml --branch main --event workflow_dispatch --status queued` as well as `--status in_progress`), because test.yml's per-event/ref `cancel-in-progress: true` cancels pending runs too.
evidence: .github/workflows/test.yml:36-40: group: test-${{ github.event_name }}-${{ github.ref }}; cancel-in-progress: true
Plan checks only `--status in_progress`
Evidence class: Partially-verified — the concurrency semantics come from the repo's workflow file; the gh `--status` values (queued/in_progress) were not observed via --help in this environment
findings.finding: The concurrency guard before dispatch checks only `gh run list --workflow test.yml --status in_progress`. test.yml uses `concurrency: group: test-${{ github.event_name }}-${{ github.ref }}` with `cancel-in-progress: true` (lines 36-40). A new dispatch on main therefore cancels any other workflow_dispatch run on main in the same group, including one that is queued and not yet in_progress. A queued dispatch, such as someone else's main-health click, is missed by the check and gets cancelled.
findings.location: Approach step 1 ('first checking `gh run list --workflow test.yml --status in_progress`')
scenarios: Another operator's 'is main healthy?' dispatch is queued behind runner capacity when this session dispatches. The in_progress check returns nothing, the new dispatch cancels the queued run, and that reading is lost.
findings.suggested_fix: Before `gh workflow run test.yml --ref main`, run both `gh run list --workflow test.yml --branch main --event workflow_dispatch --status in_progress` and `... --status queued`, and wait until both are empty. Scheduled runs use a different concurrency group (event_name=schedule) and are not cancelled, so they need no wait.
